lessons.title: Crossing the Gap From Seed to Series A

children.text: The seed round is the easiest money a good team will ever raise. The Series A is the hardest, because it is the first time anyone checks whether the story became a business. Most seed-funded Indian startups never make this jump. They do not fail dramatically, they simply arrive at month 20 with decent revenue, an honest team and numbers that do not make anyone reach for a chequebook. This lesson is about making sure that is not you, and what to do if it is.

body.text: Seed money buys you the right to run experiments. A Series A is only available once the experiments are over and one of them worked repeatedly. The gap between those two states is not time or effort, it is evidence.

stats.label: Proof of demand

stats.label: Proof of value

stats.label: Proof of a machine

stats.context: Acquisition that does not depend on a founder closing every deal

stats.label: Proof of a company

children.text: Plan Backwards From the Series A

Most founders plan forwards: here is what we will build, and we hope it adds up. Better founders plan backwards. Decide what a Series A investor in your sector needs to see, put that at month 18, and work out what it demands of every month between now and then. The arithmetic is unforgiving and extremely useful.

body.caption: Where n is the number of months available. Compounding decides whether your plan is ambitious or fictional.

children.text: An illustrative company sits at ₹1.2 crore of ARR and believes it needs ₹6 crore to raise a credible Series A in 18 months. That is 5 times growth, which sounds manageable until you convert it: 5 to the power of one eighteenth, minus 1, is about 9.35% a month, every month, for a year and a half. Now the plan can be tested against reality. Does the channel support that? Does the hiring plan? Does the cash?

body.title: Required trajectory vs a company drifting behind (ARR, ₹ crore)

body.text: Notice where the two lines separate. By month 6 the gap is small enough to explain away, and by month 12 it is decisive. The founders who survive this are the ones who treat month 6 as the moment to change something, rather than the moment to work harder at the same thing.

body.title: What does the plan actually demand?
body.prompt: A startup has ₹1.2 crore of ARR and wants ₹6 crore in 18 months. What monthly growth rate does that require? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: The multiple needed is ₹6 crore ÷ ₹1.2 crore = 5 times. Spread over 18 months, the required rate is 5 to the power of 1 ÷ 18, minus 1, which is about 9.35% a month. Founders routinely promise 5 times growth without converting it into a monthly rate, then discover at month 9 that they never built a channel capable of compounding at 9% a month.

children.text: If the Bar Is Not Going to Be Cleared

The honest moment usually arrives around month 12 to 14, when the trend is clear and there is still enough cash to act. There are more options than founders think, and all of them are better than raising for nine months and then discovering the answer.

body.caption: Five paths when a Series A is out of reach

cells: Cut burn until revenue covers costs, then grow from cash flow
Gross margins are decent and the cuts do not kill the product
A smaller round from existing investors to reach a specific milestone
One or two clear milestones stand between you and a fundable story
Raise a smaller A, or a seed extension
Take less money at a modest valuation from a fund that fits your actual size
The business is real but growing more slowly than venture scale demands
An acquisition or acqui-hire, often by a larger player in the same space
The team or technology is worth more inside someone else's business
Return remaining cash, settle dues, close cleanly
There is no path to either profitability or a next round

children.text: A bridge is money raised between priced rounds, usually from investors already on your cap table, to buy time to reach a specific milestone. Three things decide whether it works.
"Twelve more months" is not a reason. "₹2.4 crore of ARR and CAC payback under 10 months by March" is. Investors fund a gap to a defined point, not a general extension.

Bridges are often done on a convertible instrument with a discount to the next round, which avoids setting a new price while the story is weak. Remember Lesson 3.3: the discount and any cap become real dilution when the Series A finally happens.

Existing investors joining is a strong signal to outsiders. Existing investors declining is a very loud one, and new investors will ask about it directly. If your seed fund will not put in another rupee, understand why before you go to the market.
Size it for the milestone plus a margin, not for comfort. A bridge that runs out one month before the evidence lands has achieved nothing at all.

body.label: The quiet signal investors read
body.value: Whether your existing backers are in
body.context: Insiders know the company better than anyone. When they participate in a bridge or an A, outsiders relax. When they sit out, every new investor asks why, and no answer is fully satisfying. Manage this relationship long before you need it.

body.title: Which company raises a Series A?
body.question: Four seed-funded companies are 20 months past their round. Which is most likely to raise a Series A?
options: ₹9 crore ARR, grew 1.3 times last year, one customer is 40% of revenue, founder closes every deal personally
₹4.5 crore ARR, grew 3.1 times last year, 180 customers, net revenue retention 114%, two channels working without founder involvement
₹15 crore of GMV, ₹90 lakh of net revenue, growing fast, negative contribution margin per order
₹2 crore ARR, flat for three quarters, but a signed memorandum of understanding with a large enterprise
body.explanation: The second company has all four proofs: compounding growth, retention above 100%, customers spread across a real base, and acquisition that works without the founder. The first is larger but concentrated and founder-dependent, the third is growing while losing money on every order, and a memorandum of understanding is not revenue.

body.title: Month 14, and the decision cannot wait
body.scenario: Anaya's Bengaluru SaaS company raised ₹9 crore 14 months ago. ARR has gone from ₹90 lakh to ₹2.3 crore, growing about 6% a month, with net revenue retention of 103% and CAC payback of 14 months. Cash left is ₹3.2 crore, burn is ₹45 lakh a month. Her seed investor has said informally that they would support a bridge. A Series A fund told her to come back at ₹6 crore of ARR with payback under 12 months.
body.prompt: What are her real options, and what would you recommend?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the arithmetic, because it decides everything.
Runway: ₹3.2 crore ÷ ₹45 lakh = about 7 months.
To reach ₹6 crore of ARR from ₹2.3 crore takes 2.6 times growth. At the current 6% a month that needs about 16 months, which is more than double her runway. At 9% a month it takes about 11 months. Either way she cannot get there on existing cash.
So the options are:
1. Bridge to the milestone. She needs roughly 12 to 15 months of runway to reach ₹6 crore with a margin, which at current burn means about ₹6 crore. That is a large bridge relative to a ₹9 crore seed, so expect the investor to ask for cuts alongside it.
2. Bridge plus efficiency. Cut burn to around ₹35 lakh, raise ₹4 crore to ₹4.5 crore, and improve CAC payback from 14 months towards 10, which is itself one of the Series A fund's two conditions. This is the strongest version, because it fixes a stated objection rather than only buying time.
3. Raise a smaller Series A now from a fund whose bar matches a ₹2.3 crore, 6% a month business. Less dilution drama, lower valuation, and a real possibility worth testing in parallel.
4. Get to default alive. At ₹2.3 crore ARR with ₹45 lakh of monthly burn, profitability is a long way off unless the cuts are severe, so this is a fallback rather than a plan.
Recommendation: option 2, started this month. Seven months of runway means the bridge must be agreed within about six weeks, since negotiating from three months of cash removes every choice she has. She should also fix the payback number first, because a bridge raised while the underlying economics are unchanged usually just delays the same conversation by a year.

body.title: The 90 days before you open a Series A process
steps: Rebuild 18 to 24 months of monthly data: revenue, new versus repeat, by channel and by cohort.
Reconcile every metric to the audited accounts, so no number moves during diligence.
Close last year's audit and clear any statutory dues, ROC filings and foreign investment reporting.
Refresh the cap table with all convertible instruments modelled through conversion.
Write the one-page narrative: what you tested, what worked, what you will do with the money.
Fix the single weakest metric a fund will attack, whether that is payback, churn or concentration.
Name the leadership hires the round funds, and start the conversations before you raise.
Line up your existing investors: confirm who is participating and how much, before outsiders ask.

body.text: Do not spend nine months running a Series A process that the data cannot support. Each pass becomes part of your record, funds talk to each other, and a company that has been in the market for three quarters carries a discount. It is far better to withdraw, fix the two metrics that drew the objections, and return with a short sharp process.

body.title: The round between rounds
body.textWithBlank: A smaller round raised from existing investors to reach a specific milestone before a priced round is called a ___ round.
body.explanation: A bridge funds the gap to a defined milestone, not a general extension. It is usually structured as a convertible instrument with a discount, and whether existing investors join is a signal outsiders read closely.

cards.definition: The jump from proving something might work to proving it works repeatedly and can absorb much more capital.
Setting the Series A bar at month 18 and deriving the monthly growth rate and hiring plan it requires.
Reaching profitability on current growth and costs before cash runs out, which turns raising into a choice.
Money raised between priced rounds, usually from insiders, to reach a defined milestone.
Whether existing investors participate in the next round, which outsiders treat as information about the company.
An additional seed-stage round at a similar or modestly higher price, when the Series A bar is still out of reach.

points: Most seed-funded Indian startups never raise a Series A, and the reason is usually evidence rather than effort.
A Series A needs four proofs: compounding growth, retention, a channel that works without the founders, and a real company with clean books.
Plan backwards. Convert the target into a required monthly growth rate, because 5 times in 18 months means 9.35% every month.
Watch the gap between required and actual at month 6, when it is still small enough to fix.
If the bar is out of reach there are five paths: default alive, a bridge, a smaller round, a sale, or a deliberate wind-down.
A bridge must buy a defined milestone, and the discount or cap on it becomes real dilution later.
Whether existing investors participate is the loudest signal in the market, so manage that relationship long before you need it.
Never run a nine-month Series A process the data cannot support. Withdraw, fix the weakest metric, and come back with a short process.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Series A expectations, growth rates and payback thresholds vary widely by sector, business model and funding conditions, and are not standards. Anaya's company and all figures are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
